blocks.text: JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 1
Meaning and Nature of Jurisprudence
Short Revision Note

Jurisprudence is the systematic study of the basic principles and concepts of law. It asks what law is, how legal rules acquire authority, and how law relates to justice and society. Salmond described it as the “science of first principles of the civil law.”

Nature. Jurisprudence is theoretical because it studies the ideas behind legal rules. It is analytical because it clarifies concepts. It also examines how law develops and, in some approaches, whether legal rules are just or effective.
Scope. It covers sources of law, concepts such as rights and ownership, and the relationship of law with the State, morality and society.
Illustration. A tenant may have lawful possession of a house while the landlord retains ownership. Jurisprudence explains how these legal concepts apply to the same property.
Recall cue. What is law? Where does it come from? What does it do?
Exam Practice

rows: Define jurisprudence and state its subject matter in two points.
Distinguish the nature of jurisprudence from its scope.
Define jurisprudence and discuss its nature, scope and subject matter. Adapted from the 2025 Punjabi University paper.

blocks.text: 11-mark plan. Define jurisprudence and cite Salmond. Explain the nature of the subject with three or four features. Discuss its scope under sources, basic concepts, purposes and its relationship with society. Add the lease illustration and conclude with the value of studying foundational concepts.
Common mistake. Repeating the same points under both headings. Nature concerns how the subject studies law. Scope concerns what it studies.
Self Test
1. What does Salmond mean by the first principles of law?
2. How can two people have ownership and possession of the same house?
Answers. 1. The foundational principles and concepts underlying specific rules. 2. The landlord may retain ownership while the tenant has lawful possession under the lease.
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 1
Meaning and Nature of Jurisprudence
Detailed Study Note
Meaning

Contract law teaches when an agreement can be enforced. Jurisprudence asks a broader question about the idea underlying enforcement. What does it mean to say that one person has a legal right against another? The same question can arise in contract, property and constitutional law.

Salmond’s definition refers to first principles. These are the foundational concepts on which particular rules rest. For example, a rule allowing an owner to recover property assumes that we understand ownership and its relationship to possession. In Salmond’s formulation, civil law refers broadly to the law administered by the State’s courts.
Nature

rows: Studies the ideas underlying legal rules, such as authority, obligation and responsibility.
Clarifies concepts and their relationships, such as a right held by one person and a duty owed by another.
Examines how rules develop through custom and institutions and how they operate in society.
Examines whether legal rules are just and whether they serve their purposes.

blocks.text: Consider a practice that a community has followed for generations. A historical inquiry asks how it developed. An analytical inquiry asks what conditions it must satisfy to qualify as a legal custom. An evaluative inquiry asks whether recognising the practice would serve justice.
Scope and Subject Matter
• Nature and purposes of law. What gives a rule legal authority? How does law protect rights and resolve disputes?
• Sources of law. How do legislation, judicial precedent and custom contribute to the development of legal rules?
• Basic legal concepts. What do rights, duties, legal personality, ownership, possession and property mean? How do they relate?
• Law and society. How do morality, history and social conditions influence law? How does law affect society in return?
Hypothetical Illustration

Meera owns a house and leases it to Asha, who moves in. Meera retains ownership and Asha has lawful possession under the lease. This shows how different legal interests can coexist in the same property.
Reading. P. J. Fitzgerald (ed.), Salmond on Jurisprudence.
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 2
Purpose and Functions of Law
Short Revision Note

The purpose of law is the aim it seeks to achieve, such as peace, justice, protection of rights and social welfare. The functions of law are the ways it pursues those aims. Law sets standards of conduct, creates rights and duties, resolves disputes, limits public power and provides remedies when rights are infringed.
Recall cue. Set rules → protect rights → settle disputes → limit power → enable change.
Illustration. A customer pays for a refrigerator that never arrives. Law gives the parties a framework for making the agreement, defines their obligations and provides a way to seek a remedy.
Indian example. Article 39A links equal justice with free legal aid. Section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 sets out eligibility categories for legal services.
Exam Practice

rows: Distinguish purpose from function with one example.
Explain how law helps people resolve disputes.
Discuss the principal purposes and functions of law with suitable examples.

blocks.text: 11-mark plan. Define purpose and function. Explain five functions under separate headings, with an example for each. Link Article 39A and section 12 to equal access to justice. Explain how competing purposes may be balanced and close by linking legal rules, institutions and remedies to their aims.
Common mistake. Reducing the functions of law to punishment. Include a way law enables people to act and a way it limits public power.
Self Test
1. When a speed limit is set to reduce accidents, which part is the purpose and which is the function?
2. What distinction does the legal aid example illustrate?

Answers. 1. Reducing accidents is the purpose. Setting and enforcing the limit is a function. 2. Equal access to justice is the purpose. Providing a framework for eligible people to obtain legal services helps pursue it.
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 2
Purpose and Functions of Law
Detailed Study Note
Purpose and Function

Suppose a shop promises to deliver a refrigerator on Saturday. The buyer needs to know what the shop is obliged to do and what can happen if it fails to deliver. Law makes such transactions more predictable by defining obligations and providing ways to resolve disputes.

The purpose of law is the goal it seeks to achieve. A function is the work the legal system performs to pursue it. Public safety is a purpose. Setting traffic rules and enforcing them are functions that serve it. One rule can serve several purposes.
Principal Functions

rows: Sets predictable standards. Traffic rules tell drivers when they must stop and who has priority.
Defines claims and corresponding duties. A sale can give the buyer a right to delivery and impose a duty on the seller.
Provides forums, procedures and remedies. A buyer who pays for undelivered goods may seek a remedy through the appropriate forum.
Establishes institutions and limits their authority. A licensing body must act within the power given to it by law.
Lets people arrange their affairs by agreement and gives legislatures a way to address social problems, including barriers to legal assistance.

blocks.text: Indian Illustration of Equal Justice

Article 39A directs the State to promote equal justice and provide free legal aid so that economic or other disabilities do not deny opportunities for securing justice. Section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 specifies categories of persons eligible for legal services. The constitutional aim is equal access to justice. The eligibility framework helps put that aim into practice.
Balancing Competing Purposes

Hypothetical. A municipality regulates street vending. Keeping pavements accessible serves public convenience, while allowing vendors to trade supports livelihoods. Rules on designated places or times can address both interests. When discussing the purpose of a rule, identify the interests it serves and explain how its design balances them.
Authorities. Constitution of India, Article 39A. Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, section 12.
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 3
Definition Kinds and Classification of Law
Short Revision Note

Law is a system of rules and principles recognised as binding within a legal order. Austin emphasises sovereign commands and sanctions. Salmond emphasises principles recognised and applied by the State in administering justice. Classify by the question asked: source, subject, function or legal system.
Detailed Study Note

Meaning. A definition picks out what a thinker regards as central. Austin explains imposed duties through command, sovereign and sanction. His account is less natural for rules that confer powers, such as rules for making wills. Salmond’s court-centred account explains how rules operate in adjudication, while legislation also guides conduct before disputes arise.

Classification by subject. Public law concerns public institutions and their powers or responsibilities. Constitutional and administrative law are familiar examples. Private law generally regulates relationships among individuals and organisations, as in contract and tort. Criminal law belongs to public law because prosecution enforces public norms. A civil case can still involve a public-law issue.

Classification by function and source. Substantive law defines rights, duties, liabilities and offences. Procedural law supplies the machinery for asserting rights and determining liability. Legislation, precedent and recognised custom classify law by source. Domestic law operates within a State’s legal order. Public international law governs international legal relations, including relations among States.

Illustration. A tenant’s claim for return of a deposit concerns private law. The agreement and applicable rules determine whether the deposit is owed. Filing, service and hearing rules govern the process that decides the claim.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Distinguish substantive and procedural law.
11 marks. Define law and explain its major classifications.
Answer plan. introduce two definitions, classify on distinct axes, give one example per axis and end with the overlap.
Self-test. Can a rule be both legislative and procedural? Yes. A statute may prescribe the procedure for serving a summons. Avoid treating the classifications as mutually exclusive.
Further reading. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, John Austin.
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 4
Administration of Justice and Theories of Punishment
Short Revision Note

Administration of justice is the organised determination and enforcement of legal rights and liabilities through courts and other authorised institutions. Civil proceedings generally address rights and remedies. Criminal proceedings generally decide guilt and, on conviction, sentence. Punishment can serve deterrent, preventive, retributive and reformative purposes.
Detailed Study Note

Civil justice. A civil court adjudicates claims such as debt, title, breach of contract and compensation. Relief can include damages, a declaration or an injunction. In ordinary civil litigation the standard is generally balance of probabilities: the claimed fact is more likely than its opposite.

Criminal justice. Criminal proceedings determine whether the accused committed an offence. The prosecution generally bears the burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt, subject to applicable statutory rules. An acquittal and an award of civil compensation can coexist because the legal questions and standards differ.

Theories of punishment. Deterrence seeks to discourage future offending by the offender or others. Prevention or incapacitation restricts opportunities to offend, for example by imprisonment. Retribution calls for a proportionate response to past wrongdoing. Reformation seeks rehabilitation and reintegration, for example through education or treatment. Sentencing may pursue several aims within lawful limits.

Illustration. An assault may produce a criminal prosecution and a separate civil claim for injury. The criminal court asks whether guilt is proved to the criminal standard. The civil court asks whether the claimant has established liability and a basis for relief.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Explain preventive punishment.
11 marks. Distinguish civil and criminal administration of justice and explain the principal theories of punishment.
Answer plan. compare object, parties, standard and outcome, then illustrate each theory.
Self-test. Which theory focuses on changing the offender’s future conduct through rehabilitation? Reformation. Prevention focuses on restricting the opportunity to offend.
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 5
Custom as a Source of Law
Short Revision Note

A legal custom is an established practice recognised as binding. A conventional custom or trade usage may also shape terms of transactions where the law permits. Remember long and consistent observance, certainty, acceptance as obligatory, reasonableness and compatibility with controlling law.
Detailed Study Note

From practice to legal custom. Habit describes what people usually do. A legal custom requires evidence that the relevant community has accepted the practice as a governing rule. A local custom may apply to a place, while a group or family custom may be confined to a defined group. Identify the people, place and transactions to which the asserted custom applies.

Essentials and proof. A custom must be sufficiently certain for a court to determine its content and scope. Long, substantially uniform observance supports acceptance as binding. Reasonableness and compatibility with applicable legislation and public policy also matter. A party relying on a disputed custom ordinarily must plead and prove it, especially if it departs from the ordinary law.

Indian authority. In Thakur Gokal Chand v Parvin Kumari, AIR 1952 SC 231, an inheritance dispute turned on an asserted custom. The Supreme Court required long and sufficiently invariable usage showing acceptance as the governing rule, and declined to apply the English rule of immemorial usage strictly in India. Article 13(3)(a) includes custom or usage having the force of law in its definition for Article 13.

Illustration. A village proves that people often share a path by permission. That evidence supports a practice of permission. To establish a binding customary right, the claimant needs evidence of a settled entitlement, its scope and how it was consistently exercised.
Exam Practice
3 marks. What is a legal custom?
11 marks. When does a custom become law?
Answer plan. define, distinguish the kinds, apply the essentials, explain proof and cite Gokal Chand.
Self-test. Does numerical age alone establish a custom? No. Consistency, certainty and acceptance as a governing rule matter.
Judgment text. https://indiankanoon.org/doc/1388066/
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 6
Judicial Precedent
Short Revision Note

Precedent is an earlier judicial decision used to resolve a later case. The ratio decidendi is the legal principle necessary to decide the issue on the material facts. Obiter dicta are observations beyond what the decision requires. Article 141 makes law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in India.
Detailed Study Note

Finding the ratio. Start with the material facts, identify the legal issue and ask which legal proposition was necessary to reach the result. A later court can distinguish a case where a material fact or governing provision changes the legal issue. Distinguishing leaves the earlier rule in force for cases it governs.

Operation in India. The Supreme Court’s declarations of law bind all courts in India under Article 141. A High Court’s decisions bind subordinate courts within its territorial jurisdiction, subject to higher authority. Decisions from other High Courts may persuade. In Central Board of Dawoodi Bohra Community v State of Maharashtra, (2005) 2 SCC 673, a Constitution Bench explained that a smaller Bench must follow a larger Bench and that doubts may be addressed by seeking an appropriate reference.

Merits and limits. Precedent supports predictability, equal treatment and continuity. It can also produce complex lines of authority, leave old rules in place and make it difficult to identify the exact ratio. A binding precedent may be overruled by a court competent to do so. An appeal that reverses the result in the same case is a different procedural event.

Judicial development. Courts interpret statutes, resolve gaps and develop principles while deciding concrete disputes. A judge’s reasoning can shape later cases. Constitutional text, legislation, hierarchy and the issues properly before the court constrain that work.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Distinguish ratio and obiter.
11 marks. Discuss the operation, merits and limits of precedent in India.
Answer plan. define, explain ratio, explain Article 141 and hierarchy, cite Dawoodi Bohra, and discuss judicial lawmaking.
Self-test. Can a smaller Supreme Court Bench overrule a larger Bench? No. It must follow the larger Bench and can seek an appropriate reference.
Authority. Constitution of India, Article 141. Central Board of Dawoodi Bohra Community (2005) 2 SCC 673.
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 7
Legislation
Short Revision Note

Legislation is the deliberate enactment of legal rules by a competent lawmaking authority. Primary legislation takes the form of Acts of Parliament or State Legislatures within their constitutional fields. Subordinate legislation includes rules and regulations made under powers conferred by a superior law.
Detailed Study Note

Primary legislation. Traditional textbooks contrast supreme with subordinate legislation. In India, describe parliamentary and State enactments as primary legislation and explain constitutional supremacy. Legislative competence depends on the Constitution, including Articles 245 and 246 and the Seventh Schedule. A primary statute can be reviewed for breach of constitutional limits.

Subordinate legislation. A legislature may set the policy and confer authority to prescribe details, such as forms, standards or procedures. The rule-maker must stay within the enabling provision and comply with applicable procedural requirements. Ultra vires means beyond legal power. A rule may be invalid if its subject or effect exceeds what the enabling law permits.

Judicial review. In Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt Ltd v Union of India, (1985) 1 SCC 641, newspaper publishers challenged measures imposing customs duty on newsprint. The Supreme Court discussed review of subordinate legislation, including inconsistency with the parent statute and manifest arbitrariness in the applicable legal sense.

Illustration. An Act authorises an authority to specify licence application forms. A rule prescribing a form fits the grant. A rule creating an independent tax requires statutory authority for that tax and may be challenged if it lacks that authority.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Define subordinate legislation.
11 marks. Distinguish primary and subordinate legislation and explain judicial control.
Answer plan. define, compare maker and source of power, give an Indian example and cite Indian Express.
Self-test. What do you check first when challenging a rule as ultra vires? Read the parent statute and identify the particular enabling provision.
Judgment text. https://api.sci.gov.in/jonew/judis/9409.pdf
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 8
Analytical School of Law
Short Revision Note

Analytical jurisprudence studies legal concepts and the structure of positive law. Austin’s account links a general command, a determinate sovereign, a duty and a sanction. It gives a clear account of many coercive rules and encounters difficulties with custom, constitutional restraints and rules conferring powers.
Detailed Study Note

Positive law. Positive law means law laid down or recognised within an existing legal order. The analytical approach clarifies what makes a rule legally valid and how concepts such as duty and sanction relate. Questions about legal existence can be distinguished from questions about moral merit.

Austin’s command theory. A command expresses a wish backed by the prospect of an adverse consequence. A general command addresses a class of conduct. Austin’s sovereign is a determinate superior habitually obeyed by the bulk of society and not habitually obedient to another earthly superior. A sanction supports the duty imposed by the command.

Strengths and criticisms. The theory explains prohibitions such as penal rules and draws attention to institutional enforcement. A rule prescribing how to execute a will confers a legal power. An invalid will usually fails to bring about the intended legal effect, which is different from punishment for disobedience. Federal distributions of power and constitutional limits also complicate the idea of one legally unlimited sovereign.

Illustration. A rule imposing a fine for prohibited parking fits Austin’s model readily. A rule enabling two people to create a valid contract instead illustrates the limits of interpreting every rule as a coercive command.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Explain Austin’s sovereign.
11 marks. “Law is the command of the sovereign.” Discuss.
Answer plan. explain the four components, illustrate, develop the criticisms and assess where the model works best.
Self-test. Which ingredient turns a wish into a command in Austin’s model? The prospect of an adverse consequence for non-compliance.
Further reading. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/austin-john/
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 9
Kelsen and the Pure Theory of Law
Short Revision Note

Kelsen explains law as a hierarchy of norms. A lower norm derives validity from a higher norm that authorises its creation. The inquiry ultimately presupposes a basic norm, or Grundnorm. Purity refers to analysing legal validity on its own terms. General effectiveness is a condition for the legal order’s validity.
Detailed Study Note

Norms and hierarchy. A legal norm prescribes what ought to happen. A regulation derives authority from an Act, and the Act is enacted under the procedures and competences laid down by the Constitution. This explains validity by reference to legal authorisation rather than an official’s personal power.

The basic norm. To avoid an endless chain, Kelsen presupposes a basic norm that gives normative significance to the historically first constitution of the legal order. The basic norm is a theoretical presupposition. The written constitution is a positive legal text and should be identified separately.

Validity and effectiveness. Validity means belonging to the legal order through the relevant source of authority. Effectiveness concerns whether rules are generally observed or applied. The legal order as a whole must be generally effective for Kelsen’s account, although one particular rule may remain valid despite occasional breaches.

Strengths and limits. The theory clarifies authorisation and helps explain why an order must be issued under a valid rule. Its abstract character makes it less helpful for explaining the influence of political choices, moral judgment and social practice on legal development.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Define Grundnorm.
11 marks. Explain and critically assess Kelsen’s Pure Theory.
Answer plan. explain purity, norms, hierarchy and basic norm, then distinguish validity from effectiveness and evaluate.
Self-test. Is the printed Constitution identical to the Grundnorm? No. The Grundnorm is the theoretical presupposition underlying the chain of legal validity.
Further reading. https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2024/entries/lawphil-theory/
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 10
Historical School of Law
Short Revision Note

The historical school emphasises the development of law through a community’s history and institutions. Savigny linked law with the Volksgeist, or common consciousness of a people. Custom often expresses early legal development, while jurists later refine and systematise the law.
Detailed Study Note

Savigny’s account. Law develops over time as a community’s institutions and practices change. Studying history helps reveal why a particular legal rule took the form it did. Savigny opposed premature codification in the nineteenth-century German debate because he believed that a code needed a mature body of legal learning behind it.

Custom and jurists. Practices accepted as binding may provide material for customary law. With a more complex legal system, trained jurists articulate principles and reconcile doctrines. The historical approach gives explanatory importance to both social practice and professional legal development.

Contribution and criticism. The school shows why transplanting a rule without regard to local institutions can create problems. It also makes it easier to understand the continuity of legal ideas over time. The notion of a single common consciousness can obscure differences within a society. Longstanding practices may require legislative reform, especially where they disadvantage particular groups.

Illustration. A long-established local practice for sharing water can help explain how a community regulates access in dry periods. Whether a court recognises the practice as legally binding still depends on proof and the applicable law.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Explain Volksgeist.
11 marks. Examine Savigny’s theory and contribution to jurisprudence.
Answer plan. explain historical growth, custom, jurists and codification, then develop two criticisms.
Self-test. Why did Savigny object to premature codification? He believed a workable code should draw on an adequately developed body of legal principles and scholarship.
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 11
Sociological School of Law
Short Revision Note

Sociological jurisprudence asks how law works in society and how it can address social needs. Roscoe Pound described law as a tool of social engineering. He distinguished individual, public and social interests and examined how legal institutions can accommodate their competing claims.
Detailed Study Note

Law in practice. The school studies the actual effects of legal rules and institutions. A procedural right that is expensive or impractical to exercise illustrates the difference between formal recognition and practical access. This approach encourages jurists to examine how people and institutions are affected.

Pound’s interests. Individual interests include personality and private claims. Public interests concern the State in its institutional capacity. Social interests include shared conditions such as general security. Classifications help identify what is at stake. They do not give a formula for resolving every conflict.

Illustration. A municipality regulates street vending. Vendors have livelihood interests, pedestrians share an interest in safe access and public authorities must manage shared space. Rules on designated vending areas and times can accommodate these claims. A sociological analysis asks whether the arrangement works in practice.

Strength and criticism. The theory links law to observable outcomes and makes competing interests explicit. The relative weight of interests can be contested. Decision-makers must also respect governing legal rules and rights when balancing claims.
Exam Practice
3 marks. What is social engineering?
11 marks. Explain Pound’s theory of interests and assess its usefulness.
Answer plan. define the approach, describe the three interests, apply the vending illustration and explain the limits of balancing.
Self-test. What does social engineering aim to do? Use legal institutions to accommodate competing interests and reduce avoidable conflict.
Further reading. James A. Gardner, The Sociological Jurisprudence of Roscoe Pound, Part I.

☐  Explain sources of law and recall Articles 13 and 141.
☐  Distinguish civil and criminal justice and the four punishment theories.
☐  Compare Austin, Kelsen, Savigny and Pound.
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 1
State and Law
Short Revision Note

The State is an organised political community exercising public authority over a population and territory. Its familiar elements are population, territory, government and sovereignty. Theories of origin include divine origin, force, social contract and historical evolution.
Detailed Study Note

Elements. Population forms the community. Territory identifies the geographical sphere of authority. Government is the institutional machinery through which authority is exercised. Sovereignty describes ultimate public authority and external independence, exercised in practice through institutions and subject to the applicable constitutional and international framework.

Origin theories. Divine origin explains authority through a religious claim. Force emphasises conquest or domination. Social contract justifies political authority through an agreement, actual or hypothetical. Evolutionary explanations trace the gradual growth of institutions from social and historical conditions. Each approach addresses a different aspect of legitimation or development.

Law and State. State institutions enact, interpret and enforce much law. Law also creates public offices, allocates authority and limits its exercise. Under a constitutional system, the government in office exercises powers defined by law. The State is the continuing legal and political community.
Illustration. After an election a new ministry takes office. The machinery and legal obligations of the State continue, while the officials entrusted with governing change.
Exam Practice
3 marks. State the elements of the State.
11 marks. Define the State and explain its elements and relationship with law.
Answer plan. define, develop the elements, outline the origin theories and illustrate constitutional limits.
Self-test. Which element refers to the institutions that act for the State? Government.
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 2
Codification
Short Revision Note

Codification is the systematic enactment of the law of a subject in an organised code. A code may collect and restate existing rules, reform them or do both. Its advantages include accessibility and consistency. Its limits include rigidity, ambiguity and the need for periodic revision.
Detailed Study Note

Meaning and forms. Codification arranges rules and definitions into a coherent legislative scheme. A consolidating code brings existing provisions together. A reforming code changes existing law as part of the process. A comprehensive code aims to cover a whole field, while a partial code addresses a defined part. The categories answer different questions and can overlap.

Merits. A systematic code gives users a starting point and harmonises scattered rules. It can standardise expressions and remove inconsistencies. Legislative debate can clarify policy choices and allow reform across a whole subject.

Demerits. Broad statutory language can leave interpretive disputes. An inflexible provision can be slow to respond to new circumstances. Legislative consolidation can also obscure exceptions if drafting is imprecise. Judges continue to interpret codes and resolve cases within their framework.

Illustration. Suppose several enactments prescribe different licensing deadlines. A code can bring these rules together and replace them with a uniform timetable. The timetable may later need amendment for online applications.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Define codification.
11 marks. Discuss the classification, merits and demerits of codification.
Answer plan. define, explain forms, balance benefits and limits, and give one example.
Self-test. Can a code consolidate and reform at the same time? Yes. It may gather existing rules and change some of them.
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 3
Legal Rights and Duties
Short Revision Note

A legal right is a legally recognised claim, liberty, power or immunity. A claim-right corresponds to a duty owed by another. The will theory stresses control and choice, while the interest theory stresses the interests protected by law.
Detailed Study Note

Elements of a claim-right. Identify the right-holder, the person owing the duty, the act or omission required, the object concerned and the source of the right. A valid agreement, for example, may give a buyer a claim to delivery and impose a corresponding duty on the seller.

Theories. Will theory associates rights with the holder’s capacity to control or waive another’s duty. Interest theory explains rights by the protection of an interest important enough to justify legal duties. Rights of young children illustrate why protected interests may matter even where the holder cannot personally exercise choice.

Classification. A right in rem is generally enforceable against persons at large, as with the owner’s claim that others refrain from trespass. A right in personam is enforceable against identified persons, as with a claim for payment against a debtor. Rights may also be proprietary or personal, and duties positive or negative depending on whether they require action or restraint.

Further distinction. In Hohfeld’s analysis, claim correlates with duty, liberty with no-right, power with liability and immunity with disability. A person’s liberty to do something and their claim that another person assist them are separate legal positions.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Distinguish a right in rem from a right in personam.
11 marks. Explain legal rights, their elements, theories and classifications.
Answer plan. define, identify the elements through one example, compare theories and classify.
Self-test. A buyer has a claim to delivery. What is its correlative? The seller’s duty to deliver in accordance with the contract.
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 4
Legal and Corporate Personality
Short Revision Note

Legal personality is the status through which law recognises an entity as capable of holding rights or duties. Human beings are natural persons. Companies are familiar legal persons distinct from their members. The position of unborn persons, deceased persons and animals depends on the purpose and provisions of the applicable law.
Detailed Study Note

Natural and special categories. Legal recognition can be purpose-specific. An unborn child may receive a conditional benefit under applicable law, commonly contingent on live birth. Death ends the person’s ordinary capacity, while legal rules can protect interests connected with the body or estate and allow some claims to survive. Animal welfare rules may impose duties on humans regardless of whether an animal has independent procedural standing.

Corporate personality. A corporation can generally hold property and contract in its own name within its legal capacity. Continuing existence can simplify ownership and transactions when membership changes. Limited liability is a separate feature of particular corporate forms. A company may incur liability through legally attributable acts of human agents.

Theories. The fiction theory treats corporate personality as a legal attribution. Concession theory stresses recognition by the State. Realist theory views an organised group as a real social entity with a distinct collective existence. Bracket or symbol theory treats the corporation as a way of organising legal relations involving individuals.

Indian authority. In State Trading Corporation of India Ltd v Commercial Tax Officer, AIR 1963 SC 1811, a government-owned company invoked Article 19 in a tax dispute. The Supreme Court held that the corporation was not a citizen for Article 19. Legal personality and constitutional citizenship are distinct.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Define legal personality.
11 marks. Explain corporate personality and its principal theories.
Answer plan. distinguish natural and legal persons, explain theories, discuss advantages and liability, and cite the citizenship example.
Self-test. Does a company’s separate personality by itself establish Article 19 citizenship? No. Personality and citizenship depend on distinct legal rules.
Judgment text. https://www.calcuttahighcourt.gov.in/Show-Judgment-File/1964~scr_1964_4_99_190_e.pdf
JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 5
Possession
Short Revision Note

Possession concerns control over a thing and the intention to hold or exercise control over it. Classical analysis calls these corpus and animus. Possession may be actual or constructive, immediate or mediate, and lawful or wrongful according to the applicable context.
Detailed Study Note

Fact and law. Possession in fact, or de facto possession, concerns effective control assessed in context. Possession in law, or de jure possession, concerns the legal recognition of possession and its consequences. Mere physical contact does not invariably establish possession. A carrier may physically handle goods while another has a legally recognised relation to them.

Kinds and acquisition. Immediate possession is exercised directly. Mediate possession is exercised through another recognised relationship, such as a bailee holding goods. Possession can be acquired by taking control or by delivery, which may be actual or constructive. Delivery of a warehouse key may transfer practical control where the facts and legal arrangement support that conclusion.

Protection and remedies. Protecting possession discourages private force, preserves stability and helps courts determine competing claims. Possessory protection may include injunctions or recovery proceedings, depending on the applicable rules. Title and possession can support distinct claims.

Indian authority. In Rame Gowda v M Varadappa Naidu, (2004) 1 SCC 769, adjoining landholders disputed possession. The Supreme Court explained that settled possession is protected against forcible dispossession and must be disturbed through due process. A fleeting intrusion is distinct from settled possession.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Explain corpus and animus.
11 marks. Explain possession, its kinds, acquisition and legal protection.
Answer plan. define, distinguish fact and law, explain types and acquisition, then cite Rame Gowda.
Self-test. Why does law protect settled possession even where title is disputed? To prevent forcible self-help and channel disputes through legal procedures.

JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 6
Ownership
Short Revision Note

Ownership is the legal relationship that ordinarily gives a person the most extensive recognised rights in relation to property. Its incidents commonly include use, management, exclusion and transfer, subject to legal limits. Possession concerns control and can be held separately from ownership.
Detailed Study Note

Incidents and classes. An owner may have power to use, exclude, lease, transfer or leave property by will, subject to applicable restrictions. Sole ownership is held by one person. Co-ownership is shared. Ownership may be vested or contingent depending on whether the entitlement is presently secured or depends on an uncertain condition. Jurisprudence also discusses legal and beneficial ownership when law recognises those distinct positions.

Acquisition. Original acquisition arises independently of an immediate transfer from a previous owner, where law recognises the facts as sufficient. Derivative acquisition comes through another’s title, as in a valid sale or gift. Rights may also devolve by succession under the applicable legal rules. Formal requirements depend on the nature of the property and the mode of acquisition.

Ownership and possession. Title can remain with an owner who hands another person physical control. A tenant may lawfully occupy the property for a limited period. When title and present control are disputed, identify the specific claim each party makes and the legal basis for it.

Illustration. Asha leaves her bicycle with a repairer. Asha remains owner. The repairer holds it in connection with the repair. Their respective entitlements depend on the arrangement and the applicable law.

JURISPRUDENCE  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 7
Property
Short Revision Note

Property can refer to an asset or to legally recognised interests in relation to it. Property includes tangible assets and intangible rights. Its principal classifications include movable and immovable, corporeal and incorporeal, and private and public.
Detailed Study Note

Meaning and kinds. A corporeal asset is material, such as land or a bicycle. An incorporeal right is intangible, such as copyright or an easement. Land is the ordinary example of immovable property. Vehicles are ordinarily movable. The applicable definition can vary with the statute. Public and private property classifications concern the legal holder, use or interest involved.

Theories. Occupation theory associates acquisition with taking control of previously unowned resources, where law recognises the claim. Labour theory links entitlement to productive effort. Utilitarian accounts ask whether rules of property promote social welfare. Other accounts explain property as an institution defined and protected by law. These theories offer explanations or justifications and do not themselves supply the legal requirements for a transfer.

Modes of acquisition. A person may acquire property through a legally recognised original acquisition, transfer by sale or gift, or devolution through succession. Prescription can result in certain rights arising after the statutory conditions are met. Always identify the property interest and the applicable legal requirements.
Illustration. An author may sell a physical book while retaining rights in the work. Ownership of the physical copy and copyright are legally distinct interests.
